slides.title: US market entry: enter in 2027 through Amazon, and earn the move into specialty retail

paragraphs.text: US market entry: enter in 2027 through Amazon, and earn the move into specialty retail

Should Onsoo enter the US market in 2027, and if so, by which route?
Prepared for CEO Park Ji-won and the board, for the March 2027 board meeting
Draft prepared November 2026 · Based solely on the planning team briefing pack. All company, competitor and market figures in the pack are fictional benchmark data.

slides.title: Recommendation: enter the US in 2027 through Amazon (Option A); turn down the 600-door retail launch and hold the Japan scale-up

paragraphs.text: Recommendation: enter the US in 2027 through Amazon (Option A); turn down the 600-door retail launch and hold the Japan scale-up

US K-beauty skincare is $3.6B and has grown 17% a year since 2021, against 5% for all facial skincare. 41% of it sells on Amazon, where Onsoo's six-month pilot already sells 14,000 units a month at 4.5 stars.

On the planning team's own inputs, A's cumulative cash bottoms out at −$1.9M, recovers to $2.4M by 2030, and keeps group margin at 9.5% or above. It is the only US route that passes the board's money tests.

B burns $20.8M by 2030 and never pays back. It also cuts group margin to 4.5% in 2027. Its two key inputs do not hold: it assumes 4.5 units per door per week where brands at Onsoo's awareness sell 2.6, and its 1.3× Amazon "halo" rests on a correlation.
J is safe but small: $7M of extra revenue and $1.8M of cash by 2030, in a market growing 1.5% a year. Management can run only one launch in 2027, and the US is the larger prize.

No route within the cash limits reaches $40M by 2030: A reaches $26M, which points to about 2032 for $40M. And payback by 2030 holds only if Amazon ad cost stays at or below ~28.5% of sales. The plan assumes 25%, the pilot ran at 28%, and scaling brands run at 32%.
Approve A with a $4M cash envelope (well inside the $18M cap) and an ad-cost guardrail. Set the retail trigger at 20% aided awareness, not 15%, and restate the US ambition as $40M by 2032.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Only the Amazon-led route passes the board's investment, payback and margin tests; no route reaches $40M of US revenue by 2030

paragraphs.text: Only the Amazon-led route passes the board's investment, payback and margin tests; no route reaches $40M of US revenue by 2030
"On the way to $40M US revenue by 2030"
Cumulative cash back to zero by end-2030
One launch, but the heaviest to run

Reading the card: A fails only the revenue ambition, which every option misses. B fails three tests even on its own optimistic inputs. J passes the money tests but builds no US business. The weak point in A is payback, which depends on the cost of Amazon advertising (slide 12).

Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Planning-team inputs as given (ACoS 25%, duty 15%, retail 4.5 units/door/week, 1.3× halo). Pre-tax, undiscounted cash; inventory at four months of landed cost.

slides.title: The US is worth entering: K-beauty skincare is a $3.6B market growing 17% a year, and 41% of it sells on Amazon

paragraphs.text: The US is worth entering: K-beauty skincare is a $3.6B market growing 17% a year, and 41% of it sells on Amazon
US sales of K-beauty facial skincare, $B
Where US consumers bought K-beauty skincare, 2025
Survey confirms the channel: 61% of US K-beauty buyers buy K-beauty most often on Amazon, vs 22% at specialty retail. 38% discovered their last new brand on TikTok, vs 17% in a store.
Use the right base: the "$5.2B US K-beauty market" figure circulated to the board includes makeup and hair care. The market Onsoo competes in is the $3.6B of skincare.
+17% a year vs +5% for all US facial skincare ($20.1B → $24.5B). K-beauty's share of the category rose from 9.5% to 14.7%.
Source: briefing pack Tables 1–2 and September 2026 survey (n=1,200 US women aged 18–44). CAGR = compound annual growth rate, 2021–25.

slides.title: The Amazon pilot shows real demand: monthly sales nearly doubled in six months, with ratings and repeat purchase in line with benchmarks

paragraphs.text: The Amazon pilot shows real demand: monthly sales nearly doubled in six months, with ratings and repeat purchase in line with benchmarks
Pilot units sold per month, 2026 (three SKUs)
7,400 → 14,000 units a month; $4.0M a year run-rate at $24
Top complaint (6% of reviews): Korean-only label text. Fix it in the 2027 setup
In line with the 31% first-year benchmark on Amazon US; below Onsoo Korea at 48%
On a small budget. The plan assumes 25%; brands scaling from $5M to $20M run at 32%
Month-on-month growth slowed from ~17% (Feb–Apr) to ~9% (May–Jun). The 2027 plan of 300,000 units is 1.8× the June run-rate of 168,000 a year, with seven SKUs instead of three.
Source: briefing pack §6 (pilot January–June 2026, three SKUs, sold by a cross-border seller). ACoS = Amazon ad spend as a share of Amazon sales.

slides.title: Recent entrants: the one retail-first brand lost $21M and was delisted; Amazon-first brands lost far less, but only one in three reached scale

paragraphs.text: Recent entrants: the one retail-first brand lost $21M and was delisted; Amazon-first brands lost far less, but only one in three reached scale
Removed from shelves in 2025; est. cumulative US loss $21M
A national retail launch without awareness is the costliest way to fail
~$30M US revenue in 2025; added 300 retail doors in 2025
Amazon can carry a brand to ~$30M; retail came after scale, not before
…but the downside is a small business, not a $21M loss

Implication: Amazon-first is the lower-risk way in, and the route that worked for Saebom. Whether Onsoo becomes a Saebom or a Gaon Lab depends on two measurable things: ad cost at scale and repeat purchase. Both go into the 2027 guardrails (slide 16).
Source: briefing pack Table 9 (public reporting and interviews). Four brands is a small sample: read as direction, not proof.

slides.title: Retail earns more per unit than Amazon ($7.55 vs $4.73), but its extra $7.5M a year of fixed cost would take ~4,200 doors to cover; B plans 600–1,000

paragraphs.text: Retail earns more per unit than Amazon ($7.55 vs $4.73), but its extra $7.5M a year of fixed cost would take ~4,200 doors to cover; B plans 600–1,000
Why the higher unit margin does not rescue retail

Fixed cost is the problem. B adds $6.0M a year of national retail marketing and $1.5M of field sales on top of A's $2.1M base. At 4.5 units per door per week a door earns ~$1,770 a year, so covering $7.5M takes ~4,200 doors. At the 2.6 that brands at Onsoo's awareness sell, it takes ~7,400.

Amazon's lever is ad cost. Each point of ACoS costs $0.24 per unit. At the pilot's 28%, contribution falls to $4.01; at the 32% benchmark, to $3.05. Before advertising, Amazon earns $10.73 a unit, so unit contribution only turns negative above 45% ACoS.
Tariff exposure is modest. A rise in duty from 15% to 25% adds $0.35 a unit in either channel.
Doors needed to cover $7.5M a year of retail fixed cost
Source: briefing pack Tables 4 and 6. Rice Ferment Barrier Cream, applied to all SKUs as the planning team does. Landed cost = ex-factory $3.50 + freight + 15% duty on ex-factory.

slides.title: On the planning team's own inputs, retail-led breaches the $18M cap and never pays back; Amazon-led bottoms out at $1.9M and pays back in 2030

paragraphs.text: On the planning team's own inputs, retail-led breaches the $18M cap and never pays back; Amazon-led bottoms out at $1.9M and pays back in 2030
B is still losing $1.9M a year in 2030. Its cumulative loss of $20.8M is about what Mooncrest lost ($21M).
A's outflow is small and short: the 2027 setup and the inventory build, then positive cash flow from 2028.

Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Cumulative pre-tax US cash flow including inventory build; Japan (J) shown for comparison, as given in Table 7 (no working capital provided).

slides.title: Retail-led would pull group operating margin below the 8% floor for three years running, to 4.5% in 2027; Amazon-led stays above 9%

paragraphs.text: Retail-led would pull group operating margin below the 8% floor for three years running, to 4.5% in 2027; Amazon-led stays above 9%
B's 2027 US loss of $8.7M takes more than half of the ex-US group's $15.4M operating profit.
A costs the group 1.5 points of margin in 2027 and adds to margin from 2028.
A stays above 8% in every stress case we ran: its lowest is 8.7%, at 38% ACoS and 25% duty.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Group = ex-US plan ($140–158M revenue at 11.0% operating margin) plus the option's revenue and operating result.

slides.title: Retail-led assumes 4.5 units per door per week; brands at Onsoo's awareness sell a median 2.6, below the 4.0 at which the leading retailer delists

paragraphs.text: Retail-led assumes 4.5 units per door per week; brands at Onsoo's awareness sell a median 2.6, below the 4.0 at which the leading retailer delists
First-year units per door per week, by brand's aided awareness among category buyers
Onsoo sits in the lowest band. Aided awareness is 4% among US skincare buyers and 9% even among K-beauty buyers.
At that awareness, even a top-quartile brand (3.4) sells below the 4.0 bar. The leading retailer reviews newcomers after 12 months, so a 2027 launch would most likely be delisted in 2028.
The 4.5 figure comes from the retailer's deck on successful newcomers. It describes the winners, not the typical brand.
Mooncrest shows the cost: 450 doors in 2023, removed in 2025, and an estimated $21M lost.
Source: briefing pack Table 8 (retail analytics firm, 2025, 46 newcomer brands; first-year sell-through), §10 survey (Sept 2026), Table 9.

slides.title: The 1.3× Amazon halo rests on a correlation, not cause and effect; and retail-led fails the cash tests even if the halo is real

paragraphs.text: The 1.3× Amazon halo rests on a correlation, not cause and effect; and retail-led fails the cash tests even if the halo is real
Why a 0.71 correlation does not show that retail drives Amazon
Common cause. Strong brands with bigger budgets win more doors and more Amazon sales. Both follow from brand strength, so neither need cause the other.
Reverse direction. Retailers recruit brands that are already winning online. Saebom added 300 doors in 2025 only after reaching ~$30M on Amazon.
No before-and-after. A snapshot of 30 brands cannot show what happened to Amazon sales after a brand entered stores.
Shoppers point the other way. Only 17% of K-beauty buyers found their last new brand in a store; 38% found it on TikTok.
The memo's claim: "Across 30 K-beauty brands, doors correlate with Amazon sales (0.71). Retail drives Amazon sales; that is where the 1.3× halo comes from."

To pay back by 2030, B would need a halo of about 3.1×, not 1.3×: Amazon sales of 0.9M units in 2027, against 0.3M planned for Amazon-led and 5.5× the pilot's June run-rate. Even then, group margin would fall to 5.7% in 2027.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Correlation from the independent board member's memo (30 brands). Halo = B's Amazon units as a multiple of Option A's.

slides.title: Amazon-led's weak point is payback: it pays back by 2030 only if ad cost stays at or below ~28.5% of sales, against a 32% median for scaling brands

paragraphs.text: TESTING OPTION A: THE PAYBACK RISK
Amazon-led's weak point is payback: it pays back by 2030 only if ad cost stays at or below ~28.5% of sales, against a 32% median for scaling brands
Option A: cumulative cash at end-2030, $M, by Amazon ad cost (ACoS)

Payback is the test at risk. It breaks even at ACoS of 28.6%, or 26.9% if duty rises to 25%. At the 32% benchmark, A is $2.3M short at end-2030, and on 2030's cash flow it would take until about 2032–33 to pay back.
The cap and the margin floor hold in every case. Even at 38% ACoS and 25% duty, peak outflow is $7.5M (cap $18M) and group margin stays at or above 8.7%.
Volume matters less. At 25% ACoS, A still breaks even by 2030 with 20% fewer units.
So the plan must manage ad cost: grow only as fast as ACoS allows, and hold it at or below 28% (slide 16).
Amazon ACoS (ad spend as % of Amazon sales)

Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Option A volumes as planned (0.3M → 1.1M units). Duty applied to all four years in the 25% case (decision due mid-2027). Agency benchmark: brands scaling $5M → $20M on Amazon US.

slides.title: No route within the cash limits reaches $40M by 2030; Amazon-led reaches $26M, so we suggest restating the target as $40M by 2032

paragraphs.text: No route within the cash limits reaches $40M by 2030; Amazon-led reaches $26M, so we suggest restating the target as $40M by 2032
A reaches $26.4M in 2030, two-thirds of the way. It is still growing 29% a year; at that pace it would pass $40M in about 2032.
B's $37.6M would come only on its optimistic inputs, at a cumulative cost of $20.8M and three failed board tests.
Hitting $40M on Amazon alone by 2030 would need 1.67M units, 50% above plan, and buying that volume would push ACoS up.
Our suggestion: keep the cash, payback and margin tests as set, and restate the ambition as "$25M+ in 2030, $40M by 2032".

Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Retail revenue at wholesale ($14 per unit), i.e. Onsoo's revenue. The ~2032 date for $40M is a simple extrapolation of A's 2030 growth rate, not a forecast.

slides.title: The Japan scale-up is safe but small: $7M of revenue and $1.8M of cash by 2030, in a market growing 1.5% a year

paragraphs.text: The Japan scale-up is safe but small: $7M of revenue and $1.8M of cash by 2030, in a market growing 1.5% a year
The Head of Japan is right that J is safer. If US ad cost goes to benchmark, J ends 2030 ahead on cash by about $4M.
But J is capped. Onsoo already holds 3.1% of a market growing 1.5% a year.
The bandwidth rule covers 2027 only. We suggest revisiting the Japan scale-up for 2028, once the US launch is stable.
No: Japan is already 24% of sales

Trade-off for the board: J gives up about $19M of 2030 revenue, and the US platform behind it, to avoid a downside of about $4M of cumulative cash by 2030. Both cases sit far inside the $18M cap. We think the US is the better use of 2027, provided ad cost is managed.

Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Option J from Table 7 (30% contribution, $0.8M a year fixed cost, $1.0M one-time). "A at 32% ACoS" is the benchmark stress case from slide 12.

slides.title: Treat specialty retail as an option to earn, not a 2029 date: raise the awareness trigger to 20% and redesign retail costs to fit payback

paragraphs.text: Treat specialty retail as an option to earn, not a 2029 date: raise the awareness trigger to 20% and redesign retail costs to fit payback
In the 10–20% band the median brand sells 3.5 units/door/week, below the 4.0 delisting bar. Above 20% the median is 4.6.
The plan passes $10M in 2028. Sales bought with heavy advertising do not prove the brand.
Repeat at the first-year benchmark shows the brand holds customers, not just wins trials.
Retail case pays its own way and keeps 2030 payback
At $7.5M a year of fixed cost, retail needs ~4,200 doors. A test of ~300 doors (Saebom's scale) needs a matching, smaller budget.
Decide at end-2028 on the gates
A's planning case leaves only $2.4M of cash headroom at 2030, so a full-cost national launch in 2029 would break payback.

We agree with the CEO's sequence: Amazon first, retail later. Two changes would avoid a Mooncrest-style retail entry: a higher awareness bar, and a retail plan sized to what the US business can already fund.
Source: briefing pack §4 (CEO hypothesis), Tables 6, 8, 9; team analysis. Proposed gates are our recommendation.

slides.title: Launch Amazon-led in 2027 with a small cash envelope and quarterly guardrails that slow spending if ad cost or repeat purchase falls short

paragraphs.text: Launch Amazon-led in 2027 with a small cash envelope and quarterly guardrails that slow spending if ad cost or repeat purchase falls short
Form US entity; take the three SKUs back from the cross-border seller
US-compliant English labels for all SKUs (fixes the 6% complaint); MoCRA registration
Hire the US team ($0.9M a year); set up FBA inventory (~4 months of stock)
Launch four more SKUs on Amazon; plan of 300,000 units ($7.2M)
Off-Amazon marketing ($0.7M) aimed at TikTok, where 38% of K-beauty buyers discover brands
Twice-yearly awareness survey to track progress to the 20% retail gate
ACoS ≤ 28%; if above 30% for two quarters, slow paid growth and re-forecast payback
Cumulative cash within a $4M envelope; board approval needed to go beyond it
Mid-2027 tariff decision: if 25%, payback needs ACoS ≤ 27%; review pricing
US tariff decision: re-plan if duty rises to 25%
First full board review vs guardrails

Why a $4M envelope: it covers A's peak outflow in the benchmark-ACoS case ($3.2M) with some headroom, and is less than a quarter of the $18M cap. Anything beyond it would signal the plan is off track, which is the moment for the board to decide whether to push on, slow down or stop.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis. Envelope, guardrail levels and triggers are proposals for board approval.

slides.title: Five decisions for the March 2027 board meeting

paragraphs.text: Five decisions for the March 2027 board meeting
Approve US entry in 2027 through the Amazon-led route (Option A).
Only route that passes the investment, payback and margin tests
Approve a $4M envelope for cumulative US cash outflow, with board review before going beyond it.
Covers the benchmark-ACoS case; under a quarter of the $18M cap
Decline the 600-door national retail launch for 2027; adopt the retail gates (20% awareness, ACoS ≤ 28%, repeat ≥ 31%, self-funding retail case).
B fails three board tests; sell-through and halo assumptions do not hold
Restate the US ambition as "$25M+ in 2030, $40M by 2032".
No route within the cash limits reaches $40M by 2030
Hold the Japan scale-up in 2027 and revisit it for 2028.
Bandwidth allows one launch in 2027; Japan upside is ~$7M of revenue
Risk the board accepts with decision 1: payback by end-2030 is likely on the planning inputs but not assured. It needs ACoS at or below ~28.5%, against 28% in the pilot and 32% for scaling brands.
Source: Onsoo briefing pack (fictional benchmark data); team analysis.

slides.title: Method, and the judgement calls made in preparing this document

paragraphs.text: Method, and the judgement calls made in preparing this document
Read as a 2030 US revenue target. If the board meant "a trajectory toward $40M", A's $26M growing 29% a year may already satisfy it.
Retail revenue counted at wholesale ($14), the price Onsoo receives; Amazon at $24. Shelf-price revenue would overstate B.
Pre-tax, undiscounted; operating result less inventory build (four months of landed cost). No receivables or payables, which would make B worse (retailer terms).
Doors sell for the full year they are listed; fixtures paid in the year a door opens. Delisting after 12 months is not modelled, which flatters B.
25% duty applied to all four years, although the decision is due mid-2027; conservative for both options.
Ex-US plan (11.0% margin) plus the option's revenue and operating result. Japan option used exactly as given in Table 7.
The $4M envelope, ACoS guardrails and 20% awareness gate are our proposals, derived from the pack's benchmarks.
A and B volumes used as given. The pilot supports 2027 (1.8× the June run-rate with seven SKUs instead of three); later years are untested.
Charts are drawn as native shapes, so they can be edited but are not linked to data. Model figures can be regenerated from the build script.
All inputs from the briefing pack; no outside data used. Where the pack was silent or ambiguous, the choices listed here were made; all are open to challenge.
